per_item.reference: All three, then, and each one alone would have stalled it. Give me two things: the inside measurements, and the ages of the birds you want to put in it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

draws.answer: Then you are near the right size, but not the correct size for both groups at the same time. The commercial model works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre and 12 to 15 growers per square metre, so seven by four is about 56 to 84 birds. But the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference builds its model on 60 breeding hens and 60 cockerels, and on 50 breeders and 50 growers, so 7 by 4 is well under the commercial minimum and under the grower minimum. Two things to check before you start: the floor, which has to hold 420 birds at 14 by 14 cm, and the walls, which have to hold 1.5 m of racks, since that is what the commercial model uses for the 80 hens and 80 cocks. Ask ICAT about the extension for the size that fits both, and ask ANSAT for the building itself.

Then you are close, and the reference does not give you the minimum size for a henhouse. Its 2020 commercial plan counts a commercial unit at 24 to 30 hens and 6 cocks, and its 2017 village compendium counts a family henhouse at 60 hens and 6 cocks. So the reference gives a minimum of 60 breeding cocks at the commercial model, and your building is a little short of it. What is the size of the birds you really want to put in it? That is what the commercial size is built for, so I can give you something the village compendium does give you. Tell me also whether you want to run the brooder with the chicks, which is compulsory for both and saves fuel, and whether you plan to hatch in an incubator, which gives you the cocks you would otherwise need to choose.

per_item.reference: No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

per_item.reference: No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.

history.content: Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

draws.answer: Six cycles is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference works on, not a schedule of how long each bird spends at each stage. It gives a growth rate of 55 days for the cock, a hatching time of 21 days, a nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks in its 2020 evaluation; the same reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks over two years, and then counts 3,487,181 FCFA in year two. The two things that do shorten your time are the larger hatching and the culling. The cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and the hens are the ones to look after in the morning and evening. And the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the same about selling: record every expense and compare it with the income so you know when the money comes in.

It is closer, but the figure is not a rule. The six production cycles in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference are: about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. So six cycles is what keeps the egg laying and lets you sell at the time the market asks for it. What it means for the sale is that you set the batch, not the batch itself: eggs are collected every day, kept seven to ten days at most, and set pointed end down, kept seven to ten days at most.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: A faint buzzing on tomato leaves together with yellowing means whitefly is present, so you must first turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants to confirm. After that, shake the plant and look before you spray, because the wrong name wastes spray and money. Then pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies, and a strong jet of water to dislodge aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. This advice is for all market-garden areas.

The first thing to do is turn the leaves over and count the insects on the underside of a few tomato plants; a high count indicates whiteflies or aphids. Then shake each tomato plant and inspect it before you treat, because the wrong name wastes spray and money. Next, pick off the most heavily infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies, and a strong water jet to dislodge aphids while encouraging ladybirds and lacewings. If the attack is severe, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer: Year 1: legumes, the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen. Year 2: maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot. Year 3: a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year 4: an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year 1. The rule is maize at the head of the rotation, then a legume, then a root crop, then an undemanding crop.

Year 1 maize, year 2 legume, year 3 maize, year 4 fallow. The order is the cycle and not the crop: the maize is the hungry plant that takes a lot, so it goes at the head of the rotation with a legume that feeds the soil with nitrogen, then back to the soil with the fallow. So the legumes follow the maize in year one, then the fallow in year two. The maize is the crop that consumes the most of the resources and the most of the labour.

per_item.reference: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. For lowland or irrigated fields, apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then split 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, giving half at tillering and half at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. If you need variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. Weed the seedlings 2 to 3 times while they remain small. After the harvest, apply 100 kg per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 to the field and then spread urea at 100 kg per hectare in a pocket 5 to 10 cm from each seedling, making sure it does not touch the stem. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. For any variety or rate questions, see ICAT.

Transplant the seedlings after about 21 days, placing two to three plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. One week after transplanting apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15. Then split the urea applications: 100 kilograms per hectare in the first weeding stage, followed by 50 kilograms per hectare at panicle initiation, and leave 50 kilograms per hectare as the top-dress. Weed the field first at 15-25 days and again at about 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering through harvest. For variety matching and rate advice, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: My old maize field in Kara shows pale yellow older leavees while the new ones stay green, is it a pest?

draws.answer: The pattern shows the maize is experiencing nitrogen shortage in the soil. Start by reading the leaves: the uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves means the plant is hungry for nitrogen, not suffering from a pathogen. Then, avoid purchasing a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's advice because mineral fertilizer alone often gives no extra yield on exhausted soils. Next, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Then, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

per_item.reference: Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.

history.content: The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

draws.answer: That is why the compartment is built that way. The improved traditional henhouse of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is a room with a shared yard for the breeders, a chick room, and a grower compartment with a yard for the adults, and the empty end is where the chicks spend most of their time. That is the reason the spacing is one end, one end for the breeders. Build the chick room with fewer openings than the rest of the henhouse to keep the warmth in and the noise out. Keep the feeders and waterers in the same compartment.

Then the building needs a gas incubator, and the gas is supplied from a fume pipe. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says that in order to hatch for sale, you must hatch for a living, otherwise the incubator is not worthwhile. Build the chick room with fewer openings than the adult compartment so the warmth stays in, since the eggs hatch in 21 to 25 days, and keep the mother hen inside. Make the brooder for the chicks with a low wall, three bricks at most, and keep it close to the henhouse. Put a gas heater inside the chick room as well for warmth, and make sure the chicks do not stand too close to the adults.

per_item.reference: The symptom is nitrogen loss in maize, not a disease that requires roguing. Start by opening a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

history.content: After a heavy shower my corn's lower leaves are pale, especially where water pooled. Should I remove the plants?

draws.answer: That symptom indicates nitrogen loss in maize, not a pathogen attack. Open a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the plot. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying roughly 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burning. Maintain the second weeding and earthing-up at the regular schedule. If you later observe streaks or dead-hearts, seek help from ICAT.

The pale colour shows nitrogen loss, not a disease. First, open a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the field. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant to avoid burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If streaks or dead-hearts appear, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

history.content: My nanny goat's left flank is tight, she stopped grazing and looks like she is struggling to breathe.

draws.answer: Your nanny goat is suffering from bloat, which can cause a rapid loss of appetite, gas or even collapse. Get the goat up and moving while keeping its head raised to help it belch. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Immediately call the veterinary service because severe cases need their urgent help.

Your nanny is suffering from bloat, which is gas or froth trapped in the rumen after a sudden change to lush wet pasture or too many legumes, and it is an emergency. Get the goat up and moving while keeping its head raised so it can try to belch the gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service right away because a severe case needs their immediate intervention. The veterinary service is the appropriate authority to contact.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

history.content: My cows are looking weak, they have yellow urine and seem to lag behind the herd.
Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?
Yes, their gums and eyelids are pale.

draws.answer: Your cattle likely have gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown but not red, which indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick animals in the shade, provide clean water, and avoid making them walk because they are short of red blood cells. Hand-pick any ticks you see on every animal in the herd, not just the sick ones. The veterinary service will supply the proper treatment.

Your cattle have nagana, a trypanosomiasis spread by tsetse fly bites. First, keep the animals well fed and give them plenty of water so they can stay strong. Second, stop grazing them in riverine bush where tsetse flies bite, especially during the biting hours. Third, consider fly control measures to reduce exposure. Finally, you need to see the veterinary service for diagnosis and the appropriate trypanocide.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The brochure says to do it when the price is high, in the lean season, and to sell as a group or through a cooperative, so that the larger buyers can reach you. First, know your local market and what is asked for. Then, prepare the beans well and clean them, and keep them dry because damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Next, weigh the bag and compare it with the market price you would get if you sold as a group. If you still see a low price, look at other markets or whether a cooperative or ICAT can help you reach bigger buyers.

Selling after you have a good harvest is the opposite of what the brochure says. Tell me how many beans you have, because a single bag is the test. Then tell me what you are buying for: is it grain, oil or animal feed, and at what price, and whether you are selling alone or through a cooperative. Those are the four things the catalogue asks for a sale to be successful, and the beans are on the last of them.
